newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Traders, economists say Thai rates must come down.
newsitem.headline: Traders, economists say Thai rates must come down.

text.p: News the Thai baht was to be subject to a managed float was accompanied by a two percentage point hike in domestic rates and economists and traders said this could spell more gloom for the battered Thai economy.
When the managed float of the baht was announced on Wednesday, the discount rate -- the rate at which the central bank lends to commercial banks -- was raised to 12.5 percent from 10.5 percent.

"I think, in terms of the macro-economic story here, that rates have to come down," Bill Belchere, head of Fixed Income and Economic Research at Merrill Lynch in Singapore told Reuters Financial Television.

"Its hard to see how local interest rates will come down without a remerging of the onshore and offshore (foreign exchange) markets so that there is an adequate supply of dollars in the economy," Belchere added.

The Thai baht was attacked last May when speculators decided that the combination of a high current account deficit, economic and financial market woes and rumours of instability in the Thai cabinet were good reason to sell the currency.

The Bank of Thailand saw the attack off, but at a cost of some four billion dollars of its foreign exchange reserves and the creation of a two-tier exchange market -- one for onshore banks and the other for offshore banks.
Subsequently the baht traded higher offshore than onshore since the Bank of Thailand was withholding baht funding for offshore banks, or making it hugely expensive to borrow baht.
"Over time (this two tier) system has to be eliminated. It's just a question of when they decide to do it and on what terms they decide to do it," Belchere told RFTV.

He said the Thais could adopt a Singapore-style system where traders could not short the currency or they could "re-unify the system totally and get on with...addressing the problems in the financial and trade sectors".
Belchere said he felt Thai rates would have to come down within "the next quarter or so. Otherwise, I think that deepens the economic slowdown".
A senior foreign exchange trader at a European bank, who declined to be identified, agreed that interest rates had to come down.

"High interest rates to defend a battered currency is the last thing the Thai's want," he said. "The economy's already slowing down. Interest rates should be coming down, not going up. What's clear is that they're going to have get rid of the two-tier system sooner or later."
